passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the education fair hall as Akash, in a bright college blazer, leaned over the table. "Guaranteed placement, madam. Deposit today by six, or the seat goes to the next student." It was already ten to five. Aparna's palms were damp, and the brochure named no company at all. "I'll pay after I've shown my father," Aparna said. "Then you lose it," said Akash, smiling less. Aparna's phone was at nine percent, but enough to call Papa. "Don't pay anything tonight," Papa said. "We'll ask at your school and visit the college." Aparna slid the brochure into the bag. "Thank you, no."

qa.q: By what time was the deposit due?
qa.a: The deposit was due that day by six.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling at the table, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aparna felt nervous and pressured; the damp palms and the need to call Papa show it.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who is pushed to pay money today?
qa.a: Pause, check with parents and the school, visit the place and never pay under pressure. 🤍

qa.q: How might Akash see Aparna's refusal?
qa.a: As a lost quick sale; smiling less after "Then you lose it" suggests annoyance that the pressure did not work.

grounding: An admissions agent promises guaranteed jobs and pushes a same-day deposit; Aparna pauses and verifies with Papa.

passage:
Dear Devika didi,

Something happened at the education fair today and I need your advice before Papa gets home.

A man at a stall said his college gives a "hundred per cent guaranteed job" after the hotel management course. He showed photos of students in suits. Then he said there are only three seats left at the special rate and I must pay a deposit today, or I'll lose it. He kept pushing a form at me and saying, "Decide now, beta, your future is waiting."

I almost called Papa to send the money. My heart was racing. But something felt off. Why would a real college need an answer in ten minutes?

I took the brochure and said I'd come back. He looked annoyed.

Can you check if this college is real and recognised? You did your course in Pune, you'd know. I'll also ask the career counsellor at school tomorrow. I'm not paying anything until we all look at it together.

Love,
Aditi

qa.q: How many seats did the man say were left at the special rate?
qa.a: He said there were only three seats left at the special rate.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when the man pushed the form?
qa.a: Aditi felt pressured and nervous, with a racing heart, and almost called Papa to send money.
Taking the brochure, leaving, and asking Devika didi, Papa and the school counsellor to check worked, because it slowed things down and brought in trusted people.

qa.q: How might Devika didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Devika didi would likely feel relieved and proud that Aditi paused instead of paying under pressure.

grounding: It shows a teen pushed by an admissions agent to pay a deposit today for guaranteed jobs, who pauses, asks others to verify and does not rush the money decision.

passage:
You asked me to talk about the career fair scam at assembly, so here it is. I'm Urmila, Class 12.

Last month my mother and I went to a college fair at a hotel. At one stall, a very smooth man told us their aviation course had "guaranteed placement with airlines." He said if we paid a deposit that same day, I'd get a scholarship. "Offer closes at six," he said, tapping his watch.

My mother was almost ready. I could see her reaching into her bag. My stomach was tight. I kept thinking, this feels too fast.

So I said, "Can we take the papers home?" He got cold. "Then the seat will go." We left anyway.

That night my friend Himani's father, who works in admissions at a real college, looked at the papers. The college wasn't recognised. Two families from our colony had already paid.

So my one line for everyone is: if someone says decide in an hour, walk away and check.

qa.q: What time did the man say the offer closed?
qa.a: He said the offer closed at six.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling as Urmila's mother reached into her bag?
qa.a: Urmila felt anxious, with a tight stomach, sensing that the offer was moving too fast.

qa.q: What went right at the stall, and why?
qa.a: Urmila asked to take the papers home, which slowed the pressure and let a knowledgeable adult check before any money was paid.

qa.q: How might the two families who already paid feel now?
qa.a: They would likely feel cheated and upset, and perhaps embarrassed that the pressure worked on them.

grounding: It shows a teen pushed by an admissions agent to pay a deposit the same day for guaranteed placement, who pauses and gets the offer verified before any money changes hands.
